## CLINICAL RECOMMENDATION

Based on Cochrane-level evidence, single-visit and multiple-visit root canal treatment yield equivalent long-term outcomes (radiographic healing, tooth survival, flare-up incidence) for necrotic teeth with apical periodontitis, so the choice can be guided by clinician preference, case complexity, and patient factors [[PMID:36512807]]. Clinicians should counsel patients that single-visit treatment carries a modestly higher risk of pain within the first week, particularly for vital cases and when mechanical instrumentation is used [[PMID:36512807]]. When contamination cannot be adequately controlled in one visit (e.g., persistent exudate, difficult isolation, complex anatomy with a large lesion), a multiple-visit approach with calcium hydroxide interappointment dressing remains a reasonable and evidence-supported option [[PMID:9477818]] [[PMID:38243912]].

---

## EVIDENCE SUMMARY

**Cochrane Reviews**

The 2022 Cochrane review by Mergoni and colleagues is the highest-tier evidence and directly addresses this question. Pooling 47 RCTs with 5,693 analysed teeth, the authors found no difference between single-visit and multiple-visit protocols for radiographic failure at ≥12 months (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.81–1.07; 13 studies, 1,505 teeth; moderate certainty), tooth extraction, flare-up, analgesic use, or sinus tract persistence [[PMID:36512807]]. However, a higher proportion of participants reported pain within the first week after single-visit treatment (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.14–2.09; moderate certainty), with subgroup analysis suggesting this effect was concentrated in vital teeth and cases treated with mechanical instrumentation [[PMID:36512807]]. The review explicitly excluded studies that did not meet modern standards of care (rubber dam, NaOCl irrigation), strengthening applicability to contemporary practice.

**Level I — RCTs and Systematic Reviews**

The ESE 2023 Quality Guidelines endorse single-visit root canal treatment as appropriate for most cases, consistent with the Cochrane conclusion (ESE-QG-2023). A recent multicentric RCT by Simon et al. (n=160, 24-month follow-up) treating primary and secondary cases in a single visit with calcium silicate sealers reported 24-month success rates of 86.6%–87.7%, providing further contemporary support that single-visit outcomes are favourable when technique is optimised [[PMID:40491343]]. Cryotherapy and adjunctive laser therapies have been shown in RCTs and meta-analyses to reduce postoperative pain [[PMID:40297278]] [[PMID:39287434]], which may be particularly useful when single-visit treatment is selected for necrotic cases with symptomatic apical periodontitis.

**Level II — Prospective Studies**

Almeida et al. designed a three-arm prospective RCT protocol comparing single-visit, two-visit with Ca(OH)₂ dressing, and two-visit without dressing in mandibular molars with asymptomatic apical periodontitis, evaluated by CBCT at 24 months — outcome data are pending but the design reflects continued clinical equipoise [[PMID:36635764]].

**Level IIIa — Retrospective Cohort Studies**

The large single-operator private-practice cohort by Jurič and colleagues (1,259 teeth, up to 13 years follow-up, 91% recall) identified single-visit treatment as an independent predictor of reduced success at the tooth level (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.21–0.75) using strict PAI ≤2 criteria [[PMID:38243912]]. This contrasts with the Cochrane pooled finding and likely reflects case-mix (a mix of complex referred cases with pre-existing apical periodontitis) rather than a true protocol effect; per the PRISMA dedup rule, the Cochrane synthesis takes precedence, but this cohort usefully signals that in complex necrotic cases with large lesions, multiple visits may still be prudent. Vieira et al. similarly found that a higher number of visits without interappointment medicament negatively influenced outcome, suggesting that if multiple visits are undertaken, an intracanal medicament should be used [[PMID:38214429]].

**Classic / Foundational**

The mechanistic rationale for multiple visits derives from Sjögren et al., who showed that when a post-instrumentation culture was negative before obturation, 5-year healing reached 94%, versus only 68% when residual bacteria were detectable — a statistically significant difference [[PMID:9477818]]. The authors argued that reliable elimination of bacteria before obturation cannot always be achieved in a single visit without an interappointment antimicrobial dressing. Sjögren's earlier long-term study confirmed that pulp necrosis with periapical radiolucency healed in only 86% of cases (vs >96% for vital cases), underscoring that necrotic cases with apical periodontitis are the group in which infection control is most consequential [[PMID:2084204]]. These microbiological findings are the basis for continued advocacy of a multiple-visit protocol in selected complex necrotic cases, even though modern RCTs pooled in the Cochrane review show equivalent clinical/radiographic outcomes.
